## The Framingham Heart Study <img src="map.png" height="120px" style="vertical-align:middle;"> 
*  *Long-term*, **Multigenerational**, study conducted in *Framingham Massachusetts* from 1948-present 

::: {.info-box}
 <ul >
    <li class="fragment"><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i>The study aimed to help identify common factors in Cardiovascular Disease</li>
    <li class="fragment"><i class="fa-solid fa-bowl-food"></i>Primary outcome: incident coronary heart disease (CHD), defined as first-onset CHD events during follow-up.</li>
    <li class="fragment"><i class="fa-solid fa-link"></i>Details can be found [here](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(13)61752-3/fulltext).</li>
</ul>
:::


## The Dataset

*  The dataset was accessed from [kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/aasheesh200/framingham-heart-study-dataset)

::: {.info-box}
<ul>
  <li class="fragment"><i class="fa-solid fa-table"></i> Dimensions: <strong>4,240 rows</strong> and <strong>16 variables</strong>.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><i class="fa-solid fa-triangle-exclamation"></i> Missingness proportions were highest for: <strong>Glucose (9.15%)</strong>, <strong>Education (2.48%)</strong>, <strong>Blood Pressure(1.25%)</strong>, and <strong>Total Cholesterol (1.18%)</strong>.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><i class="fa-solid fa-magnifying-glass-chart"></i> Other predictors with missingness: <strong>Cigarettes/Day (0.68%)</strong>, <strong>BMI (0.45%)</strong>, and <strong>Heart Rate (0.02%)</strong>.</li>
</ul>
:::

- This missingness pattern motivates using **MICE** to retain observations and reduce bias from complete-case analysis. <img src="missing_pattern.png" style="height:90px; vertical-align:middle; margin-left:10px;">

## MICE <img src="MICE.png" style="height:80px; vertical-align:middle; position:relative; "> <span class="mice-cite"><a href="https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v045i03">Van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn(2011)</a></span> {.mice-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.mice-box}
<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><strong>Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE)</strong> fills missing values by iteratively modeling each incomplete variable using the others.</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Here we set variable-specific methods (<code>norm</code>, <code>logreg</code>, <code>polr</code>) and keep <code>TenYearCHD</code> as a predictor without imputing it.</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="4">The algorithm cycles through incomplete variables until values stabilize.</p>

:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="58%" data-fragment-index="2"}
```{r des}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-3|5-14|16-20|"
init <- mice(train_data, maxit = 0, print = FALSE)
meth <- init$method
pred <- init$predictorMatrix

meth[] <- ""
meth["cigsPerDay"] <- "norm"
meth["BPMeds"] <- "logreg"
meth["education"] <- "polr"
meth["totChol"] <- "norm"
meth["BMI"] <- "norm"
meth["heartRate"] <- "norm"
meth["glucose"] <- "norm"
meth["TenYearCHD"] <- ""
pred["TenYearCHD", ] <- 0

framing.imputed.train <- mice(
  data = train_data, m = 20, method = meth,
  predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 214, maxit = 5
)
train_complete <- complete(framing.imputed.train)
```

::: {.info-box .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
<ul>
  <li><strong>Data split:</strong> 70% train, 30% test.</li>
  <li><strong>Why MICE:</strong> preserves sample size and reduces complete-case bias.</li>
</ul>
:::
:::
:::


## Pooling, Tree Fitting, and Test Evaluation

::: {.info-box}
<ul>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Pooling after imputation:</strong> fit models across imputed training datasets and combine estimates/predictions to reduce Monte Carlo noise.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Training stage:</strong> all tree-based models are fit on the <strong>70% imputed training set(s)</strong>.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Evaluation stage:</strong> final performance is assessed on the <strong>30% imputed test set</strong> using confusion matrix, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.</li>
</ul>
:::

- Models fit in this project: <strong>Pruned Decision Tree</strong>, Random Forest, BART, and Ridge Regression (benchmark).


## Classic Decision Tree  {.tree-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.mice-box}
<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><strong>Classification Decision Trees</strong> use a top-down, greedy approach known as recursive binary splitting.</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3">We use the Gini index for binary splits, this measure of inequality, was first introduced by Italian Statistician Corrado [Gini](https://ourworldindata.org/what-is-the-gini-coefficient) in 1912</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="4">We can evaluate our trees performance using a variety of metrics, we will assess the results of all our approaches at the end of this lecture</p>

:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="58%" data-fragment-index="2"}
```{r tree}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-7|9-11|12-19|"
library(tree)
tree_prob_list <- vector("list", length(train_all))
for (i in seq_along(train_all)) {
  tree_fit_i <- tree(TenYearCHD ~ ., data = train_all[[i]])
  p_i <- predict(tree_fit_i, newdata = test_all[[i]], type = "vector")
  tree_prob_list[[i]] <- p_i[, "1"]
}

tree_cm <- table(Predicted = tree.pred, Actual = tree_actual)
tree_cm

tree_accuracy <- mean(tree.pred == tree_actual)
tree_misclass <- 1 - tree_accuracy
tree_sensitivity <- tree_cm["1", "1"] / sum(tree_cm[, "1"])
tree_specificity <- tree_cm["0", "0"] / sum(tree_cm[, "0"])
```

::: {.info-box .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
<ul>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Build the tree</strong> in the training data.</li>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Evaluate performance</strong> in the test set.</li>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Overfitting</strong> is a major issue in this naive        approach, pruning helps to combat this.</li>
</ul>
:::
:::
:::

## Random Forest  {.rf-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.mice-box}
<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><strong>Random Forest is an ensemble method:</strong> it combines many decision trees built on bootstrap samples to produce a stronger overall model.</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"> For classification, each tree votes and the final class is the <strong>majority vote</strong>. Averaging over many trees reduces variance and improves prediction stability.</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="4"> At each split, only a <strong>random subset of predictors</strong> is considered (often <code>m ~ sqrt(p)</code>), so trees are less similar and averaging works better.</p>
:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="58%" data-fragment-index="2"}
```{r rf}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-6|8-10|12-17|"
library(randomForest)
Framing.rf <- randomForest(
  TenYearCHD ~ ., data = train_complete,
  mtry = floor(sqrt(ncol(train_complete) - 1)),
  ntree = 500, importance = TRUE
)

rf_pred <- predict(Framing.rf, newdata = test_complete)
rf_cm <- table(Predicted = rf_pred, Actual = test_complete$TenYearCHD)
rf_cm

rf_accuracy <- mean(rf_pred == test_complete$TenYearCHD)
rf_sensitivity <- rf_cm["1", "1"] / sum(rf_cm[, "1"])
rf_specificity <- rf_cm["0", "0"] / sum(rf_cm[, "0"])
rf_oob_error <- Framing.rf$err.rate[nrow(Framing.rf$err.rate), "OOB"]
```

::: {.info-box .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
<ul>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Training:</strong> fit the forest on imputed training data.</li>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Testing:</strong> evaluate confusion matrix and sensitivity/specificity on test data.</li>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>OOB error:</strong> internal estimate of test error from out-of-bag observations.</li>
</ul>
:::
:::
:::

## BART <img src="Bart_Simpson.png" style="height:90px; vertical-align:middle; position:relative; "> Bayesian Additive Regression Trees {.bart-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.mice-box}
<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><strong>BART combines ideas from bagging/RF and boosting:</strong> trees are built with randomness, but each tree also captures signal not yet explained by the current ensemble.</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><strong>Relation to other methods:</strong> unlike bagging/RF (independent trees) and unlike pure boosting (strict sequential fitting), BART blends both in a Bayesian framework.</p>

<p class="fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><strong>Flexible use:</strong> BART can be used for both regression and classification; here we use binary classification for <code>TenYearCHD</code>.</p>
:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="58%" data-fragment-index="2"}
```{r bart}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-4|6-8|10-13 |"
library(BART)
x_train <- train_complete %>% select(-TenYearCHD)
x_test  <- test_complete %>% select(-TenYearCHD)
y_train <- as.numeric(as.character(train_complete$TenYearCHD))

bartfit <- pbart(x.train = x_train, y.train = y_train, x.test = x_test)
bart_prob <- bartfit$prob.test.mean
bart_pred <- factor(ifelse(bart_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))

bart_cm <- table(Predicted = bart_pred, Actual = test_complete$TenYearCHD)
bart_accuracy <- mean(bart_pred == test_complete$TenYearCHD)
bart_sensitivity <- bart_cm["1", "1"] / sum(bart_cm[, "1"])   
bart_specificity <- bart_cm["0", "0"] / sum(bart_cm[, "0"])
```

::: {.info-box .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
<ul>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Training:</strong> fit Bayesian tree ensemble on imputed training data.</li>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Prediction:</strong> convert posterior mean probabilities to classes.</li>
  <li><i class="fa-solid fa-bullseye"></i><strong>Evaluation:</strong> assess confusion matrix, sensitivity, and specificity on test data.</li>
</ul>
:::
:::
